note: Four synthetic projects. Each is a decision record built up over time, the way a team's IRP ledger would be. Some decisions supersede earlier ones; many name the options turned down.

decisions.what: Use PostgreSQL as the primary datastore for all services.
decisions.why: Payments need ACID transactions across several tables, and finance needs relational reporting.
decisions.alternatives: MongoDB: rejected, no multi-document transactions we trust for money. DynamoDB: rejected, vendor lock-in.

decisions.what: Internal services talk to each other over REST with JSON.
decisions.why: Simplest option for a team of three.
decisions.alternatives: gRPC: rejected for now, tooling overhead.

decisions.what: Store money as integer minor units (cents) and do all money arithmetic through the ledgerly-money library.
decisions.why: Floating-point rounding errors caused a reconciliation mismatch in the prototype.
decisions.alternatives: Decimal strings: rejected, parsing everywhere.

decisions.what: Webhook deliveries retry with exponential backoff, up to 5 attempts, then are marked failed.
decisions.why: Keeps the delivery queue short.

decisions.what: Feature flags live in an in-house config table.
decisions.why: Customer data must stay in the EU, and the hosted flag services we looked at were US-only.
decisions.alternatives: LaunchDarkly: rejected, US data residency.

decisions.what: Internal services talk to each other over gRPC.
decisions.why: Latency between the ledger and risk services became the bottleneck.
decisions.alternatives: Keeping REST over HTTP/2: rejected, measured and not fast enough.

decisions.what: Redis is used only as a cache, never as the source of truth for any balance or record.
decisions.why: In the February incident Redis evicted keys under memory pressure and balances had to be rebuilt.
decisions.alternatives: Redis with AOF persistence as a store: rejected, still not durable enough for money.

decisions.what: Version the public API in the URL path (/v1/, /v2/).
decisions.why: Our clients are banks with slow upgrade cycles and fixed gateway configurations.
decisions.alternatives: Header-based versioning: rejected, several bank gateways strip custom and Accept headers.

decisions.what: Webhook deliveries retry for up to 24 hours (8 attempts) before they are marked failed.
decisions.why: Partner banks have maintenance windows of up to 12 hours.

decisions.what: Every pull request touching the ledger service needs a review from the payments team.
decisions.why: The ledger is the system of record.

decisions.what: Feature flags and gradual rollouts use Unleash, self-hosted in our EU region.
decisions.why: The in-house table couldn't do percentage rollouts; self-hosting keeps data in the EU.

decisions.what: Design tokens are defined in Figma variables, which are the single source of truth, and synced to code.
decisions.why: Designers own the tokens and work in Figma every day.
decisions.alternatives: Defining tokens in code and syncing to Figma: rejected, designers lost ownership and edits drifted.

decisions.what: The primary brand colour is Fjord Blue (#1F4FD8).
decisions.why: Matches the 2025 brand guidelines.

decisions.what: Icons come from Material Symbols.
decisions.why: Broad coverage and free licence.
decisions.alternatives: A custom icon set: rejected for now, cost.

decisions.what: Body text is never smaller than 16px.
decisions.why: Our accessibility audit flagged 14px text as hard to read for many users.

decisions.what: Dark mode is built with token modes, not separate stylesheets.
decisions.why: One set of components, switched by mode.
decisions.alternatives: A separate dark stylesheet: rejected, doubles maintenance and drifts.

decisions.what: Use Inter as the typeface everywhere, including exported PDF reports.
decisions.why: Reports must render identically on every machine.
decisions.alternatives: System fonts: rejected, PDF reports rendered inconsistently across operating systems.

decisions.what: At most one primary button per view.
decisions.why: Usability tests showed users hesitated when two actions looked equally important.

decisions.what: Icons come from the in-house Fjord Icons set.
decisions.why: The brand refresh needed a distinctive icon style; Material looked generic.

decisions.what: Spacing follows a 4px base scale.
decisions.why: Aligns with the token grid.

decisions.what: The primary brand colour is Fjord Teal (#0F766E).
decisions.why: Fjord Blue failed contrast in dark mode and clashed with a competitor's identity.

decisions.what: Batch pipelines are Airflow DAGs that run nightly at 02:00 UTC.
decisions.why: Retries and visibility that cron scripts lacked.
decisions.alternatives: Cron scripts: rejected, no retries or visibility.

decisions.what: Customer email addresses are hashed before they enter the warehouse; analysts only ever see the hash.
decisions.why: GDPR data minimisation: analysts don't need raw emails.
decisions.alternatives: Raw emails protected by column-level access rules: rejected, one misconfigured role exposes everything.

decisions.what: Dashboards are built in Metabase.
decisions.why: Free and quick to set up.
decisions.alternatives: Tableau: rejected, licence cost.

decisions.what: Raw event data is kept for 13 months.
decisions.why: Year-over-year comparisons.

decisions.what: Transformations are written in dbt.
decisions.why: Testable and versioned.
decisions.alternatives: Stored procedures: rejected, untestable.

decisions.what: No streaming infrastructure: everything is batch or micro-batch.
decisions.why: We are a three-person team and nobody needs data fresher than 15 minutes.
decisions.alternatives: Kafka: rejected, operational cost far beyond our team's capacity.

decisions.what: Pipelines are Dagster assets.
decisions.why: Asset-based lineage and testing; the Airflow DAGs had sprawled.
decisions.alternatives: Staying on Airflow 2: rejected, DAG sprawl.

decisions.what: Every new source table needs a data contract before it is loaded.
decisions.why: Unannounced schema changes broke three pipelines last quarter.

decisions.what: Dashboards are built in Superset.
decisions.why: We now need row-level security per region, which Metabase couldn't do for us.

decisions.what: Raw event data is kept for 6 months.
decisions.why: Legal review of our consent wording.

decisions.what: Users sign in only through their company's single sign-on (SAML or OIDC).
decisions.why: We don't want to store or protect passwords.
decisions.alternatives: Our own username and password login: rejected, security burden and liability.

decisions.what: Salaries are visible only to HR and the employee's own manager.
decisions.why: Customer policy.

decisions.what: The mobile app is built with React Native.
decisions.why: One codebase for a team of four.
decisions.alternatives: Separate native iOS and Android apps: rejected, two codebases.

decisions.what: All notifications are sent by email.
decisions.why: Simplest to build first.

decisions.what: Employee data is hosted in the EU region (Frankfurt).
decisions.why: Our customer contracts require EU hosting.

decisions.what: Leave requests are approved by the manager; requests over 10 days also go to HR.
decisions.why: HR wanted oversight of long absences.

decisions.what: Search uses PostgreSQL full-text search.
decisions.why: Our largest customer has 2,000 employees; that's small data.
decisions.alternatives: Elasticsearch: rejected, another service to run for very little gain.

decisions.what: Notifications are in-app and push; email is used only for payslips.
decisions.why: Employees told us in the survey that email notifications were overwhelming.

decisions.what: Every screen meets WCAG 2.2 AA before release.
decisions.why: Public-sector customers require it.

decisions.what: Managers approve all leave requests; HR is no longer in the approval flow.
decisions.why: HR had become a bottleneck, and an audit found no issues with manager-only approval.
